solutions.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

clue.text: Providing aid from stake money invested in silver

parts.note: Ag is the chemical symbol for silver
a stake is a bet
tin is old slang for money

explanation.surface: Someone funds a good cause by putting their gambling winnings into silver.
explanation.walkthrough: "Stake money" reads as one phrase but splits into two pieces, BET and TIN. Silver's symbol AG then opens up around both.
explanation.definitionFit: Abetting someone is helping or encouraging them, usually in wrongdoing.

clue.text: Something made a report extremely close to the truth

indicators.note: extremely means at the extremes, so only the outermost letters of the word are kept

parts.note: first and last letters of report

indicators.note: the close of a word is its end, so its last letter is taken

parts.note: last letter of the
a fact is a truth

explanation.surface: A journalist's piece that comes extremely close to the truth.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Close to the truth' reads as one phrase meaning nearly true, but 'close to' only takes the last letter of 'the', and 'truth' stands alone.
explanation.definitionFit: An artefact is an object made by human hands, such as a tool or ornament.

clue.text: Oslo's latest new premium clothes store

indicators.note: to clothe is to cover, so the rearranged letters wrap around the single letter
new means made afresh, so the letters of premium are given a different order
the latest part of a word is its last letter

parts.note: the name Oslo, whose last letter is O; the 's reads as 'is'

explanation.surface: An advert for an Oslo shop's newest premium range of clothing.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Clothes store' looks like the definition, but 'clothes' is a verb meaning dresses, wrapping the rearranged PREMIUM around O.
explanation.definitionFit: An emporium is a large shop selling many kinds of goods, a store.

clue.text: Yankee that's annoying turning up late

indicators.note: in a down answer, turning a word up makes it read from bottom to top

parts.note: Yankee is Y in the NATO phonetic alphabet
"drat!" is what you say when something annoys you

explanation.surface: An American's habit of arriving late is getting on someone's nerves.
explanation.walkthrough: "That's annoying" seems to describe the lateness, but it stands for the exclamation DRAT.
explanation.definitionFit: Tardy means slow to arrive, or late.

clue.text: Spreading concern, few seen gathering briefing papers

indicators.note: spreading the letters around rearranges them

parts.note: anagram fodder, 14 letters

explanation.surface: Worry spreads through a group while hardly anyone is seen gathering up important documents.
explanation.walkthrough: "Papers" here means newspapers: a news conference is a gathering that briefs the press.
explanation.definitionFit: At a news conference, reporters from the papers are briefed together.

clue.text: Place to buy in or sell out

definitions.meaning: a retail premises, the ordinary noun
to betray someone, as an informer does to the police; a British slang verb

explanation.surface: A trader's advice: buy stock when it is cheap, sell when it peaks.
explanation.walkthrough: "Buy in" and "sell out" look like opposite trades. In fact "sell out" means to betray, and "to shop" someone is British slang for informing on them.
explanation.definitionFit: Two senses: the everyday noun for a retail premises, and British slang for informing on someone, which betrays them.

clue.text: Suspended on railway for lacking sufficient fare

indicators.note: in a down clue on means placed after, so the second piece follows

parts.note: something suspended is hung up

explanation.surface: Someone was suspended from the railway for not having enough money for the fare.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Fare' looks like a train fare, but here it is food: hungry people lack enough to eat.
explanation.definitionFit: Fare can mean food, so someone without enough of it is hungry.

clue.text: Quietly letting agreement bring happiness

parts.note: p (piano) means quietly in music
a lease is an agreement to let property

explanation.surface: Signing a tenancy without fuss makes everyone content.
explanation.walkthrough: "Letting" seems to mean allowing, but it means renting out property, so the agreement is a LEASE.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: the verb means to give someone pleasure or satisfaction.

clue.text: Troops secured a row for snipers somehow

indicators.note: the letters come together in some other way, i.e. rearranged

parts.note: anagram fodder, 14 letters

explanation.surface: Soldiers have somehow won a line of positions for their marksmen.
explanation.walkthrough: "Secured" reads as an active verb, but in the definition it means held captive: these are troops who have been secured.
explanation.definitionFit: Prisoners of war are soldiers held captive by the enemy.

clue.text: A squealer's confession sounded sweet, but cold

indicators.note: the confession is said, so it is the sound that counts

parts.note: someone who squeals admits "I scream"

explanation.surface: An informer confesses in a voice that is sweet but chilly.
explanation.walkthrough: A squealer seems to be an informer, but it is just someone who screams. The old rhyme "I scream, you scream, we all scream for ice cream" plays on the same sound.
explanation.definitionFit: A definition by description: a frozen dessert, sugary yet chilled, and the "but" plays up that contrast.

clue.text: Jersey artist of high standing

parts.note: a jersey is a top
someone who draws is a drawer

explanation.surface: A respected painter from the island of Jersey.
explanation.walkthrough: The capital J makes Jersey look like the Channel Island, but it is the sweater. A drawer is also where a jersey is kept.
explanation.definitionFit: Top drawer means of the highest social class or quality.

clue.text: Boat staff bringing nothing on board

indicators.note: something on board is inside the vessel

parts.note: a cane is a walking staff
O looks like zero

explanation.surface: The crew of a boat bring nothing with them.
explanation.walkthrough: Staff seems to mean the crew, but it is a stick, a CANE.
explanation.definitionFit: A canoe is a small, light boat paddled by hand.

clue.text: Raid spanning a period of a year

parts.note: as in "for a year": for gives how long something lasts
kept as it is
Y is an abbreviation for year

explanation.surface: A military campaign that lasted twelve months.
explanation.walkthrough: The clue spells out the phrase "for a year", with "spanning a period of" standing in for FOR.
explanation.definitionFit: A foray is a sudden attack or raid into enemy territory.

clue.text: Car chase mostly prepared, DS means to get ready

indicators.note: prepared means made up or worked over, so the combined letters are rearranged
mostly means all but the last letter

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A detective sergeant has mostly planned a car chase, getting ready for action.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Ready' is slang for cash, so cards that get you ready money fit. DS reads as a detective sergeant in the surface but is used only for its letters.
explanation.definitionFit: Ready money, or readies, is British slang for cash, and cash cards let you withdraw it from machines.

clue.text: Look back on gas sanctions

parts.note: a countenance is a face or look

indicators.note: the back of a word is its last letter

parts.note: last letter of GAS, placed after

explanation.surface: Someone reflects on the sanctions placed on gas supplies.
explanation.walkthrough: "Look back on" seems to mean remember. Split it up: "Look" is COUNTENANCE and "back" takes the last letter of GAS.
explanation.definitionFit: To countenance something is to allow or approve it, so countenances means sanctions.

clue.text: What's up with MPs limiting speculation?

indicators.note: limiting means bounding on each side, so the outer word holds the reversed piece

parts.note: Tories are Conservative members of Parliament

indicators.note: in a down clue up means the word is read from bottom to top, so backwards

parts.note: eh is a cry of 'what?'; the 's reads as 'is'

explanation.surface: A puzzled question about what is going on with members of Parliament.
explanation.walkthrough: 'What's up' reads as an idiom, but 'What' is EH and 'up' turns it over. Tories are the UK Conservative Party, here standing for MPs.
explanation.definitionFit: Theories are ideas put forward without proof, which is what speculation consists of.

clue.text: Charge identified with electron

parts.note: a thing stamped is marked to show what it is
e is the symbol for an electron

explanation.surface: A physics fact: the charge that belongs to an electron.
explanation.walkthrough: Charge and electron together point to electricity. Here charge is the headlong rush of a herd.
explanation.definitionFit: A stampede is a sudden mass charge of animals or people.

clue.text: State vessel used to rescue an elite force

parts.note: Noah's ark saved the animals from the flood
kept as it is
the SAS is the British Army's special forces regiment

explanation.surface: A government ship is sent to save a crack unit.
explanation.walkthrough: "State vessel" reads as a ship of state, but "State" is the definition. The rest of the clue describes the ark.
explanation.definitionFit: A definition by example: one of the fifty US states, in the south of the country.

clue.text: What newsreaders read in French, the expert seducer conceals

parts.note: a tempter is a seducer; "the expert" is split up, see below
le is French for the
a pro is an expert

explanation.surface: A French phrase about an accomplished seducer who hides what he's up to.
explanation.walkthrough: "The expert seducer" reads as one phrase, but "the" belongs with "in French" to give LE, and "expert" is PRO.
explanation.definitionFit: A teleprompter shows the script newsreaders read on camera.

clue.text: Advantages of dogs off the lead

indicators.note: the lead is the first letter, and it comes off

parts.note: basset hounds; the B goes

explanation.surface: The benefits of letting your dogs run loose.
explanation.walkthrough: A lead is a dog's leash in the surface, but in the wordplay it is the leading letter of BASSETS.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: a useful skill or quality counts in your favour, so it is an advantage.

clue.text: Careful cutting a stem

indicators.note: cutting means removing, so the letter a is taken out of the word

parts.note: sparing means careful, economical with resources

explanation.surface: A gardener's caution about taking a cutting from a plant stem.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Cutting a stem' reads as gardening, but 'cutting' takes A out of SPARING, and 'stem' is a verb.
explanation.definitionFit: To stem from something is to spring from it, both meaning to originate or arise.

clue.text: Comic character from Peru: he's funny or contrary

indicators.note: contrary means going the other way, so OR reads backwards
funny letters are strange ones, i.e. rearranged

parts.note: anagram of PERU HES
OR backwards

explanation.surface: A cartoon figure from Peru who is either amusing or awkward.
explanation.walkthrough: "Comic character" seems to mean a funny man, but it is a character from a comic book.
explanation.definitionFit: Superheroes are the heroes of comic books.

clue.text: Dance backwards while gripping a medic

indicators.note: gripping means holding tight, so the reversed word surrounds the rest
backwards means the word is read from the end

parts.note: as can mean while, as in 'as I was leaving'
MB is Bachelor of Medicine, a doctor's degree

explanation.surface: A dancer moves backwards while holding on to a doctor.
explanation.walkthrough: MB, Bachelor of Medicine, is a common way to clue a doctor.
explanation.definitionFit: The samba is a lively Brazilian dance of African origin, associated with carnival.

clue.text: Something footballers put on skin

definitions.meaning: a British football team's shirts, shorts and socks, its kit
a verb: to peel off an outer covering

explanation.surface: Players rub something into their skin before a match.
explanation.walkthrough: "Put on skin" reads like applying cream, but the clue breaks after "on". In Britain a football team's strip is its shirts, shorts and socks.
explanation.definitionFit: Two senses: the British noun for a team's kit, and the verb for peeling off an outer layer, as you skin fruit.

clue.text: Skip over some novel ideas

indicators.note: only some of the letters of NOVEL IDEAS are used

parts.note: found inside novEL IDEas

explanation.surface: An instruction to pass over a few fresh ideas.
explanation.walkthrough: "Novel" could be a book or an anagram signal, but here it just carries the letters.
explanation.definitionFit: To elide is to omit or skip over, especially a sound in speech.

clue.text: Striking people outside that hurt colleagues

parts.note: a corker is a strikingly attractive person
"ow!" is what you say when something hurts

explanation.surface: Workers on strike wound their fellow employees who cross the picket line.
explanation.walkthrough: "Striking people" suggests workers on strike, which suits the answer. It means corkers, a British word for people who look stunning.
explanation.definitionFit: Co-workers are people who work together: colleagues.

clue.text: I'm exasperated seeing time being wasted

definitions.note: an interjection standing in for the one-word exclamation

indicators.note: being wasted means lost or thrown away, so the letter is dropped

parts.note: sight is the act of seeing

explanation.surface: Someone loses patience watching time being frittered away.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Seeing' looks like a link word but is the noun SIGHT, which loses its T.
explanation.definitionFit: Saying 'sigh' aloud, as an exclamation, signals weariness or frustration with someone.

clue.text: Forecasters for hours absorbed by "cats and dogs"?

parts.note: pro means for, in favour of

indicators.note: something absorbed by a thing is taken inside it

parts.note: cats and dogs are examples of pets, hence the question mark
h is an abbreviation for hours, taken inside PETS

explanation.surface: Weather forecasters spend hours on the phrase "raining cats and dogs".
explanation.walkthrough: "Cats and dogs" in quotes calls up the heavy-rain saying that weather forecasters use, but here it just means pets.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: those who foretell what is coming, whether seers of old or weather forecasters.
